description: This dashboard provides a Detailed/DrillDown view of the Yarn Resource manager & Node Manager status, performance, and resource usage. Metrics are scraped by Prometheus via the jmx-exporter for Yarn Resource manager/node manager deployments.

panels.title: Cluster Health Metrics

panels.description: Indicates how many nodes are currently active in the cluster.
panels.title: Number of Active NodeManagers

panels.description: This metric shows the total CPU capacity across all active NodeManagers in the cluster. It is the sum of the vCores available on each registered NodeManager. It is useful for tracking CPU resource availability and load distribution in the cluster.
panels.title: Total vCores Available

panels.description: This metric shows the total memory capacity across all active NodeManagers in the cluster. It monitors the overall memory pool available for YARN container allocation.
panels.title: Total Memory Available

panels.description: When a NodeManager is decommissioned, it means that the node is being gradually removed from the cluster. The decommissioning process allows running containers on the node to complete while preventing new allocations. This metric monitors how many nodes are currently in the process of decommissioning.
panels.title: Number of Decommissioning Nodes

panels.description: This metric counts the NodeManagers that have either Crashed, Been manually stopped, or Failed due to issues like hardware failure, network disconnection, or configuration errors. This node monitors the cluster's node availability and detecting unexpected failures.
panels.title: Number of Shutdown NodeManagers
Queue & Application Metrics

panels.description: This metric tracks the number of applications that are currently in an active state (e.g., RUNNING, ACCEPTED). It does not include applications that are FINISHED, FAILED, or KILLED. It monitors the workload and application concurrency in the cluster.
panels.title: Total Number of Active Applications

panels.description: This metric tracks applications that are actively executing tasks on the cluster. It excludes applications in other states like ACCEPTED, FINISHED, FAILED, or KILLED. It monitors real-time workload activity.
panels.title: Number of Runing Applications

panels.description: This metric tracks applications that are waiting for resource allocation but have not yet started running. These applications remain in the PENDING state until sufficient memory (MB), CPU (vCores), or other resources become available. A high number of pending applications may indicate resource contention or inefficient resource allocation.
panels.title: Number of Pending Applications

panels.description: This metric counts applications that have finished running successfully without errors. It does not include applications that were FAILED, KILLED, or currently RUNNING. It helps track workload throughput and cluster utilization over time.
panels.title: Number of Completed Applications

panels.description: This metric counts applications that have terminated due to errors or unexpected failures. Failures could be caused by: Application logic errors (e.g., exceptions in Spark, MapReduce, or other YARN applications), Insufficient resources (memory or vCore allocation failures), Container crashes, Node failures (NodeManagers going down). It helps in troubleshooting and identifying stability issues in the cluster.
panels.title: Number of Failed Applications

panels.description: This metric counts applications that were terminated before completing execution. An application can be killed for various reasons, including: Manual intervention: A user or administrator may kill an application due to problems or resource contention, ResourceManager's decision: The ResourceManager may kill an application if it exceeds certain thresholds (e.g., running out of memory, timeouts, or failure of critical tasks), Node failures: If a NodeManager crashes or becomes unavailable, applications running on that node may be killed, Application issues: An application may be killed due to internal errors, excessive resource consumption, or failed container launches.
panels.title: Number of Kiiled Applications

panels.description: A container in YARN is a unit of resource allocation (CPU, memory) that runs a task for an application. This metric tracks how many containers are currently in use across all running applications.
panels.title: Total Number of Containers Currently Allocated Across All Running Applications

panels.description: A container in YARN is a unit of resource allocation (CPU, memory) that runs a task for an application. This metric tracks how many containers are currently in use across all running applications.
panels.title: Number of Containers that Have Been Reserved But not yet Allocated

panels.description: This metric counts containers that are needed by running applications but cannot be allocated immediately due to resource constraints. High pending container counts indicate resource contention or insufficient cluster resources (CPU, memory). It can help identify bottlenecks in resource scheduling.
panels.title: Number of Containers that have been Requested by Applications But Are Still Waiting for Resource Allocation

panels.description: Tracks how many vCores are actively assigned to running applications. Used to monitor CPU utilization and detect resource bottlenecks. If this value is close to hadoop_resourcemanager_capabilityvirtualcores, the cluster is fully utilized. If it's low, the cluster might be underutilized, meaning available CPU resources are not being used efficiently.
panels.title: The total number of virtual CPU cores (vCores) currently allocated to running containers across the YARN cluster.

panels.description: This metric counts all containers that were allocated and then freed. A container is released when: A job completes and no longer needs it, The application terminates (either normally or abnormally), The ApplicationMaster (AM) requests to release it (e.g., dynamic resource scaling), YARN preempts resources to allocate them to higher-priority jobs.
panels.title: Total Number of Containers that have been Released by applications Since the ResourceManager Started

panels.description: This metric shows how much memory (RAM) is actively being used by running applications. It helps monitor cluster resource utilization and detect potential memory bottlenecks. If this value is too high (close to total cluster capacity), new applications may experience scheduling delays. If it is too low, the cluster might be underutilized, meaning available resources are not being fully utilized.
panels.title: The total amount of memory (in MB) that is currently allocated to running containers across the YARN cluster.

panels.description: This metric tracks vCores that have been reserved for scheduling but are not actively in use yet. Reservation happens when YARN's CapacityScheduler or FairScheduler holds resources for applications to prevent resource starvation. If high values persist, it may indicate inefficiencies in scheduling or long queue wait times. If low or zero, it means all CPU resources are being actively used or there is no pending demand.
panels.title: The total number of virtual CPU cores (vCores) reserved but not yet allocated
Scheduler Performance Metrics

panels.description: Node updates occur periodically when NodeManagers report their status (available resources, container statuses, health reports, etc.) to the ResourceManager. This metric helps in diagnosing performance issues related to RM-NM communication. A higher value may indicate ResourceManager overload, slow scheduling decisions, or network latency.
panels.title: Average time (in milliseconds) taken by the ResourceManager (RM) to process node updates from NodeManagers (NMs)

panels.description: Each NodeManager (NM) periodically sends heartbeat updates to the ResourceManager to report: Available resources (CPU, memory, etc.), Status of running containers, Node health information. The ResourceManager processes these updates to manage scheduling decisions and cluster resource allocation. This metric counts the total number of such node update operations since the RM started.
panels.title: Total number of node update operations processed by the ResourceManager (RM).

panels.description: When a job is submitted, YARN must allocate a container to run the Application Master (AM). This metric captures the average time spent waiting before the AM starts running. If the value is high, it means applications are experiencing delays in starting, possibly due to: Resource shortages (memory, vCores), Scheduler inefficiencies (CapacityScheduler/FairScheduler misconfiguration), Queue congestion (too many pending applications), Overloaded ResourceManager struggling to assign AM containers.
panels.title: Average delay (in milliseconds) between when an application is submitted and when its Application Master (AM) is launched

panels.description: average delay (in milliseconds) between when an Application Master (AM) is launched and when it receives its first allocated container. This metric measures how long it takes for the first container to be allocated to the AM after it starts. If this value is high, applications may be waiting too long for resources, which could be caused by: Cluster resource exhaustion (not enough memory or vCores), Queue congestion (large backlog of pending applications), Scheduler inefficiencies (CapacityScheduler/FairScheduler misconfiguration), Delays in NodeManager heartbeats causing scheduling bottlenecks.
panels.title: Average delay (in milliseconds) between when an Application Master (AM) is launched and when it receives its first allocated container.
JVM & System Health

panels.description: The ResourceManager runs as a Java process and utilizes heap memory for scheduling, tracking applications, and handling cluster resource allocation. This metric provides real-time insight into how much heap memory the RM is consuming. A high value may indicate memory pressure, potentially leading to Garbage Collection (GC) pauses or even OutOfMemory (OOM) errors.
panels.title: Amount of heap memory (in MB) currently being used by the ResourceManager (RM).

panels.description: Non-heap memory is used by Java applications for areas outside of the heap, including: Metaspace (stores class metadata), Code cache (stores compiled Java bytecode), Direct memory buffers (used for off-heap data structures). This metric tracks how much of the allocated non-heap memory the ResourceManager (RM) is actively using. If non-heap memory usage grows too high, it may indicate memory leaks or excessive class loading, leading to performance degradation or OutOfMemory (OOM) errors.
panels.title: Amount of non-heap memory (in MB) currently used by the ResourceManager (RM).

panels.description: This metric accumulates the time spent by the RM's Java Virtual Machine (JVM) in performing Garbage Collection (GC). GC is essential for memory management in Java applications, but excessive GC time can indicate memory pressure, inefficient heap tuning, or high object churn. If the value increases rapidly, it suggests that the JVM is spending too much time in GC, which may impact RM performance.
panels.title: Total time (in milliseconds) spent on garbage collection (GC) by the ResourceManager (RM) JVM process since it started

panels.description: This metric counts the number of GC events where the GC time exceeded a warning threshold, which indicates potential JVM memory pressure or long GC pauses. It helps detect excessive garbage collection, which may degrade performance, causing delays in scheduling and resource allocation. A consistently increasing value suggests that the JVM is spending too much time in GC, leading to higher latencies and potential RM instability.
panels.title: Number of times the ResourceManager (RM) has exceeded a predefined Garbage Collection (GC) warning threshold.

panels.description: This metric tracks the count of actively running threads that are either: Executing a task, or Waiting for CPU time to execute. A higher value means that more threads are competing for CPU resources, which may indicate high load or contention issues. A sudden spike in threadsrunnable might signal performance bottlenecks or thread exhaustion, while a low or stable value suggests normal operation.
panels.title: Number of threads in the "RUNNABLE" state within the ResourceManager (RM) JVM process

panels.description: This metric counts threads that are in the WAITING state, meaning they are not actively running but are waiting indefinitely for a signal or notification to proceed. Threads in this state are typically: Waiting for locks or conditions (e.g., using wait() or sleep()), Paused until another thread notifies them (e.g., via notify() or notifyAll()). A high number of waiting threads may indicate thread contention, lock-related delays, or inefficient scheduling.
panels.title: Number of threads in the "WAITING" state within the ResourceManager (RM) JVM process.
RPC & Network Metrics

panels.description: This metric measures the latency of incoming RPC (Remote Procedure Call) requests in the ResourceManager’s RPC queue. A higher value means that requests are waiting longer before being handled, which may indicate ResourceManager overload or insufficient processing capacity. A low value suggests that requests are being processed efficiently without major delays.
panels.title: Average time (in milliseconds) that RPC requests spend in the ResourceManager (RM) queue before being processed

panels.description: This metric counts the total RPC operations that have been processed by the ResourceManager. An increase in this count over time reflects that the RM is actively processing RPC requests from clients, such as applications, NodeManagers, and other components in the cluster. This value can help monitor RM activity levels and determine if it’s handling an increasing load of RPC operations.
panels.title: Total number of RPC (Remote Procedure Call) operations processed by the ResourceManager (RM).

panels.description: This metric counts the outbound network traffic generated by the ResourceManager, representing the total amount of data sent over the network to communicate with other nodes or services. It is useful for monitoring the network load on the ResourceManager, helping you identify if there are increased communication patterns, such as during large-scale job submissions, container allocation, or status updates between the RM and other cluster components.
panels.title: Total number of bytes sent by the ResourceManager (RM)

panels.description: This metric counts the inbound network traffic that the ResourceManager receives from other nodes or services. It includes: Job submissions, container requests, and status updates received by the ResourceManager, Heartbeat messages from NodeManagers and other RPC responses sent by clients or applications. Monitoring this metric is important for assessing the network load on the RM and understanding how much data the RM is handling.
panels.title: Total number of bytes received by the ResourceManager (RM).

panels.description: This metric counts the RPC requests that are considered slow based on a configurable threshold. Slow calls can occur due to various reasons: ResourceManager overload (e.g., due to high load or insufficient resources), Network issues, causing delayed responses, Slow client requests, where the request handling takes longer than usual. Monitoring this metric helps identify potential performance degradation in RPC processing within the ResourceManager.
panels.title: Number of RPC (Remote Procedure Call) requests that take longer than expected to be processed by the ResourceManager (RM).
